mcqs.question: What design goal best separates CPU and GPU architecture at the highest level?
options: CPUs optimize for latency of a single task; GPUs optimize for throughput across many tasks
CPUs use more transistors overall than GPUs
GPUs always run at a higher clock frequency than CPUs
CPUs are designed only for integer math, GPUs only for floating-point math
mcqs.explanation: Latency-vs-throughput is the root design split that explains pipeline depth, cache size, and core count differences. GPUs actually run at lower clocks, transistor totals vary by product, and both chips handle integer and floating-point work.

mcqs.question: Which workload profile is the best fit for a GPU?
options: A workload with heavy, unpredictable branching and frequent cross-element communication
A massively data-parallel workload where every element follows roughly the same control path
A single long sequential dependency chain that must execute in strict order
A workload that requires very low latency for one isolated operation
mcqs.explanation: GPUs win when the same operation applies uniformly across huge numbers of independent elements. Heavy branching, long sequential chains, and single-operation latency all favor CPU-style execution instead.

mcqs.question: A candidate says 'GPUs are always faster than CPUs for parallel-looking code.' What's the flaw in that claim?
options: GPUs cannot execute conditional branches at all, so the claim is meaningless
GPUs have less total compute than CPUs, so the claim is backwards
Heavy per-element branching or frequent cross-element communication can erode or reverse the GPU's throughput advantage even when a workload looks parallel
GPUs only support single-precision floating point, making the comparison invalid
mcqs.explanation: Surface-level parallelism isn't sufficient — divergent branching and inter-element dependencies undercut the very throughput mechanisms GPUs rely on. GPUs can execute branches (via masking), and precision support varies by hardware generation, not architecture class.

mcqs.question: Why does a GPU tolerate memory latency by oversubscribing threads instead of relying on large caches like a CPU?
options: GPUs physically cannot have caches due to die area constraints
GPU thread state is cheap to hold in registers, so switching to another ready thread while one waits on memory costs nothing, unlike a CPU context switch
GPU memory is always faster than CPU memory, so latency is never actually a problem
Thread switching on a GPU requires saving and restoring state just like a CPU, so the benefit comes only from clock speed
mcqs.explanation: GPUs keep thousands of threads resident with state held in on-chip registers, so switching to a ready thread while another waits on memory is essentially free -- no save/restore overhead like a CPU context switch. This is why occupancy (enough resident threads to always have work ready) matters so much for GPU performance, not raw memory speed or cache size.

mcqs.question: A GPU rated at 20 TFLOPS peak runs a kernel needing only 0.25 FLOP per byte moved, with 800 GB/s memory bandwidth. What limits this kernel's achieved throughput?
options: Clock speed -- lowering the GPU's clock would fix the bottleneck
Compute -- the kernel will achieve close to the full 20 TFLOPS since the GPU is powerful
Memory bandwidth -- the kernel is memory-bound, achieving only about 200 GFLOPS, roughly 1% of peak compute
Nothing limits it; peak FLOPS is always achievable regardless of memory traffic
mcqs.explanation: Achievable FLOPS for a memory-bound kernel is bandwidth times FLOPs-per-byte: 800e9 * 0.25 = 200 GFLOPS, about 1% of the 20 TFLOPS peak. The kernel never comes close to taxing the ALUs because it's starved waiting on memory traffic -- exactly the low-arithmetic-intensity case the roofline model formalizes.

mcqs.question: A workload is 95% parallelizable and 5% serial. Why doesn't a 10,000-core GPU deliver anywhere close to a 10,000x speedup?
options: Amdahl's law caps speedup based on the unavoidable serial fraction, and that portion often runs slower per-core on a GPU than on a CPU
GPUs cannot execute serial code at all, so the workload simply fails to run
10,000 cores always deliver exactly 10,000x speedup regardless of serial fraction
The serial portion automatically parallelizes itself once enough cores are available
mcqs.explanation: Amdahl's law caps achievable speedup at 1/(serial fraction) in the ideal limit -- here, at most 20x -- regardless of core count, because the serial 5% doesn't speed up at all. GPU cores being individually weaker than CPU cores makes that serial portion's cost worse, not better, which is why minimizing host-side serial work matters as much as maximizing parallel core count.
